units.title: The Bronze Age Aegean
units.blurb: Crete, the islands and mainland Greece: the Minoans and Mycenaeans, their palaces, how they are dated, and how the palaces ended.

units.title: Kinds of Writing
units.blurb: Word signs, syllables and letters; the scripts of Crete and Cyprus; and the Greek alphabet that came after them.

units.title: The Discovery
units.blurb: Arthur Evans at Knossos, Carl Blegen at Pylos, and the fires that saved the tablets.

units.title: The Decipherment
units.blurb: From Bennett's sign numbers and Kober's triplets to Ventris's grids, the 1952 breakthrough and the tablet that confirmed it.

units.title: The Linear B Signs
units.blurb: The vowels, the rows of the syllabic grid, the special signs and the signs no one has read.

units.title: How Linear B Spells Greek
units.blurb: Open syllables, missing consonants, empty vowels, shared signs and glides: the rules for getting from signs to words.

units.title: Logograms, Numbers and Tablets
units.blurb: Object signs, male and female animals, numerals and measures, the shapes of tablets, the scribes, and reading a line.

units.title: Mycenaean Greek
units.blurb: The oldest written Greek: words and their later forms, endings you can see, places and gods.

units.title: What the Tablets Tell
units.blurb: The palace economy, the wanax and his officials, offerings to the gods, and what the tablets leave out.

units.title: Linear A
units.blurb: The Minoan script: where it is found, the signs it shares with Linear B, its numbers and fractions, ku-ro, the libation formula, and why it is still unread.

units.title: Judging and Comparing
units.blurb: How to test a decipherment claim, and the two scripts side by side.

topics.title: The Aegean World
topics.short: Crete, the Cyclades and mainland Greece, linked by the sea, in the Bronze Age (about 3000 to 1100 BC).
topics.trouble: Students picture Bronze Age Greece as one country. It was a patchwork: an island civilization on Crete, island towns, and later several small palace states on the mainland.

topics.title: The Minoans of Crete
topics.short: Crete's Bronze Age civilization, named by Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos; we do not know what they called themselves.
topics.trouble: Students think "Minoan" is the people's own name or that Minos was a real, known king. The name is a modern label taken from Greek legend.

topics.title: Knossos and the Cretan Palaces
topics.short: Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros: big buildings around a central court that stored goods, held workshops and kept records.
topics.trouble: Students imagine a palace as only a royal home. Aegean "palaces" were also storehouses, workshops, shrines and record offices.

topics.title: The Mycenaeans
topics.short: Greek speakers of the mainland from about 1600 BC, with palaces at Mycenae, Pylos, Thebes and Tiryns; by about 1450 BC Greek speakers ran Knossos too.
topics.trouble: Students treat Minoans and Mycenaeans as the same people, or as Homer's heroes exactly as the poems tell them. They were different cultures, and Homer wrote centuries later.

topics.title: Dating the Aegean Bronze Age
topics.short: Periods named from pottery styles (Early, Middle and Late Minoan; Helladic on the mainland), tied to years by radiocarbon and by links to Egypt.
topics.trouble: Students read "c. 1450 BC" as an exact year. Aegean dates come from pottery sequences and radiocarbon and can be off by decades or more; some, like the eruption of Thera, are debated.

topics.title: The End of the Palaces
topics.short: Around 1200 BC the mainland palaces were destroyed, Pylos by fire, and writing disappeared from Greece for about four centuries.
topics.trouble: Students look for one cause. Scholars debate several (earthquakes, raids, warfare between states, drought and the breakdown of trade), and most think more than one played a part.

topics.title: Word Signs, Syllables and Letters
topics.short: Three ways to write: a sign for a word (logogram), a sign for a syllable (syllabogram), or a sign for a single sound (a letter of an alphabet).
topics.trouble: Students think every ancient script is picture-writing. Most ancient scripts mix word signs with sound signs, and Linear B is mostly sound signs.

topics.title: How a Syllabary Works
topics.short: One sign per syllable: a vowel alone (a) or a consonant plus a vowel (ka, ke, ki, ko, ku), so the signs fill a grid of consonants and vowels.
topics.trouble: Students treat a syllable sign as a letter. The sign ka is one sign for two sounds; there is no separate sign for k.

topics.title: Cretan Hieroglyphs
topics.short: Crete's earliest script, used mostly on seals from about 2100 or 1900 BC to about 1700 BC; it overlapped with Linear A and is still unread.
topics.trouble: Students confuse Cretan hieroglyphs with Egyptian hieroglyphs. They are a separate Cretan script, with different signs and an unknown language.

topics.title: A Family of Aegean Scripts
topics.short: Linear A gave rise to Linear B; on Cyprus, Cypro-Minoan and then the Cypriot syllabary, which wrote Greek and was read in the 1870s.
topics.trouble: Students think Linear B is the oldest Aegean script, or that it descends from the Greek alphabet. Linear B was adapted from Linear A, long before the alphabet.

topics.title: Then Came the Alphabet
topics.short: After the palaces fell no one wrote in Greece for about four centuries; around 800 BC Greeks borrowed the Phoenician letters and added vowels.
topics.trouble: Students assume the Greek alphabet grew out of Linear B. The alphabet came from the Phoenician script, after Linear B had been forgotten.

topics.title: Arthur Evans at Knossos, 1900
topics.short: Evans began digging at Knossos in March 1900, found thousands of clay tablets, named Linear A and Linear B, and believed their language was not Greek.
topics.trouble: Students assume the excavator understood what he found. Evans's firm view that the tablets were Minoan, not Greek, held back the idea that Linear B could be Greek.

topics.title: Carl Blegen at Pylos
topics.short: In 1939 Blegen found the archive room of the palace at Pylos on the first day of digging; after the war, in 1952, his team found many more tablets.
topics.trouble: Students think Linear B was found only on Crete. Pylos showed it was the script of the mainland palaces too, which helped make the case that its language was Greek.

topics.title: Clay, Fire and Survival
topics.short: The tablets were sun-dried clay meant for one season's records; the fires that destroyed the palaces baked them and saved them.
topics.trouble: Students think the tablets were fired on purpose to last. They were everyday notes in damp clay; we have them because the buildings burned.

topics.title: Numbering the Signs
topics.short: Emmett Bennett sorted the signs into a standard list; scholars still name a sign by its number, like *08, and write an unread sign that way.
topics.trouble: Students treat a sign number as a sound. *08 is only a label in a list; its value, a, came later.

topics.title: Alice Kober's Triplets
topics.short: In the 1940s Alice Kober showed that Linear B words change their endings, using sets of three related forms, without guessing any sounds.
topics.trouble: Students think Kober guessed at sounds or a language. Her method was to avoid guessing: she proved inflection and showed which signs must share a consonant or a vowel.

topics.title: Building the Grid
topics.short: Michael Ventris placed signs in a grid so that signs in one row shared a consonant and signs in one column a vowel, before knowing any of the sounds.
topics.trouble: Students assume the grid was filled with sounds from the start. It began as relationships only; sounds came last, when a few guesses unlocked whole rows and columns.

topics.title: The Breakthrough: Cretan Place Names
topics.short: Ventris tried known Cretan place names on words found only at Knossos: ko-no-so (Knossos), a-mi-ni-so (Amnisos) and tu-ri-so (Tylissos), and the grid gave Greek.
topics.trouble: Students think one lucky word proved the decipherment. A few names gave values; the test was that those values then turned many other words into Greek.

topics.title: Greek, 1952
topics.short: Ventris announced on BBC radio on 1 July 1952 that Linear B was Greek; with John Chadwick he published the case in 1953.
topics.trouble: Students imagine Ventris set out to prove it was Greek. He expected a language related to Etruscan, and the Greek results surprised him.

topics.title: The Tripod Tablet Confirms It
topics.short: On Pylos tablet Ta 641, read in 1953, the words read by Ventris's values describe the pictured vessels: ti-ri-po beside a tripod, and cups with four, three or no handles.
topics.trouble: Students think everyone agreed at once. Most specialists were convinced within a few years, but some doubted it for a long time; the tablet's match of words and pictures did much to persuade them.

topics.title: The Five Vowel Signs
topics.short: a, e, i, o and u: five signs that stand for a vowel alone, the first column of the grid.
topics.trouble: Students mix up signs that look alike, such as a and the double-axe-like signs near it. Learn each vowel with its picture-like shape.

topics.title: The d, k, m, n and p Rows
topics.short: Each row is one consonant with the five vowels: da de di do du, ka ke ki ko ku, and so on.
topics.trouble: Students expect signs in one row to look alike. Signs that share a consonant usually look nothing like each other; you learn them one by one.

topics.title: The Other Rows: j, q, r, s, t, w, z
topics.short: The rest of the grid: q for sounds like kw, r for both r and l, z for a sound like dz, and the glides j and w; some rows have gaps.
topics.trouble: Students read q as English "kw" spelled with a q and think it is a different language's sound. In Linear B, q stands for the old Greek labiovelars (kʷ, gʷ, kʷʰ), which later became p, b, t or d.

topics.title: Special Signs
topics.short: Signs beyond the basic grid: a2 (ha), a3 (ai), au, pu2 (phu), ra2, ra3, ro2, ta2, and signs for clusters like dwe, dwo, nwa, pte, twe and two.
topics.trouble: Students think the special signs are required. Scribes could usually spell the same word with the basic signs; the special signs were optional shortcuts.

topics.title: Signs Still Unread
topics.short: About fifteen rare signs, such as *18, *47 and *63, have no agreed value; a few, like *65 (perhaps ju) and *79 (perhaps zu), have proposed values.
topics.trouble: Students take unread signs as proof that Linear B is not really deciphered. The unread signs are rare; the common signs are read with confidence and make good Greek.

topics.title: Every Sign Ends in a Vowel
topics.short: Linear B can only write syllables that end in a vowel, so Greek words full of consonant clusters and final consonants must be bent to fit.
topics.trouble: Students expect the spelling to show every sound. It cannot: a sign always ends in a vowel, so many sounds go unwritten or get an extra vowel.

topics.title: Missing Consonants
topics.short: Final consonants, and l, m, n, r and s before another consonant, are not written: ka-ko is khalkos (bronze), pa-ta is panta (all), pe-mo is sperma (seed).
topics.trouble: Students read the spelled form as the whole word, as if ka-ko were said "kako". The Greek word is khalkos; the spelling leaves out sounds the reader supplied.

topics.title: Clusters and Empty Vowels
topics.short: Other consonant clusters are split with a vowel borrowed from the next syllable: ko-no-so for Knossos, ti-ri-po for tripos, a-re-ka-sa-da-ra for Alexandra.
topics.trouble: Students pronounce the empty vowel. In ti-ri-po the first i was not said; it is there only because the script has no sign for t alone.

topics.title: One Sign, Several Sounds
topics.short: r stands for r and l; p, k and q signs each cover a voiced, voiceless and aspirated sound; only d and t are kept apart; h is usually not written.
topics.trouble: Students think pa-ta must contain p and t sounds. pa could be pa, ba or pha; the reader knew from the word which one was meant.

topics.title: Diphthongs and Glides
topics.short: Between vowels the glides j and w often appear (i-je-re-u, hiereus, priest); the u of a diphthong is written (au, eu), but the i of ai, ei, oi is often left out.
topics.trouble: Students read every j or w as a full consonant. Many are glides the scribe wrote between vowels, and the i of diphthongs often disappears from the spelling.

topics.title: Logograms
topics.short: Signs for things (man, woman, horse, tripod, wheat, wine) that stand before a number and say what is counted; they are not read as part of a sentence.
topics.trouble: Students confuse logograms with syllable signs, or read a logogram as a sound. A logogram tells you what is being counted; the words before it are spelled in syllables.

topics.title: Male and Female Animals
topics.short: Small marks show the sex of animals: a ram has two short bars across its stem, a ewe a forked stem; scholars write them OVISm and OVISf.
topics.trouble: Students think the two sheep signs are different animals. They are one logogram, sheep, marked male or female.

topics.title: Aegean Numbers
topics.short: Strokes for ones, bars for tens, circles for hundreds, circles with rays for thousands; you add them up, and the order of the groups does not change the value.
topics.trouble: Students treat the numerals as place value, like our digits. Each mark has its own value and you add them, as with Roman numerals but with no subtraction.

topics.title: Weights and Measures
topics.short: Dry goods: a unit, then T (a tenth), V (a sixth of T) and Z (a quarter of V); liquids: a unit, S (a third), V and Z; weights from the talent (L) down.
topics.trouble: Students convert measures as if they were decimal. Each step has its own ratio: 1 unit = 10 T, 1 T = 6 V, 1 V = 4 Z for dry goods.

topics.title: Pages, Leaves and Labels
topics.short: Page-shaped tablets for lists, palm-leaf tablets for single entries, clay labels for baskets, sealings, and words painted on jars.
topics.trouble: Students picture all tablets as big pages of text. Many are narrow "palm leaves" with a single line about one transaction.

topics.title: Scribes and Their Hands
topics.short: Each scribe's handwriting can be recognized; scholars count about 66 hands at Knossos and 45 at Pylos and number them.
topics.trouble: Students imagine many people could write. Writing seems to have been the work of a small number of palace scribes.

topics.title: Reading a Tablet Line
topics.short: Most lines follow one pattern: a word or name, then a logogram, then a number; a word divider separates words.
topics.trouble: Students read straight through, turning the logogram into a syllable. Find the word divider, the logogram and the number first, then read the word.

topics.title: Mycenaean Words and Their Descendants
topics.short: ti-ri-po is tripous (tripod), di-pa is depas (cup), e-ra-wo is elaion (oil), wa-na-ka is anax (lord): many Mycenaean words live on in later Greek.
topics.trouble: Students think Mycenaean is a different language from Greek. It is Greek, about 500 years older than Homer's poems were written down, and some words changed sound (wanax became anax).

topics.title: Endings You Can See
topics.short: Some endings show through the spelling: -o-jo for the genitive of o-stems (te-o-jo, of the god), -e and -i for datives (di-we, to Zeus), -pi for an instrumental plural.
topics.trouble: Students expect the endings of Classical Greek. Mycenaean has older endings, like genitive -oio (written -o-jo), that Homer still uses.

topics.title: Places on the Tablets
topics.short: ko-no-so (Knossos), pa-i-to (Phaistos), a-mi-ni-so (Amnisos), ku-do-ni-ja (Kydonia, modern Chania), pu-ro (Pylos) and te-qa (Thebes) are named on the tablets.
topics.trouble: Students expect the place names to look like their modern spellings. Read them through the spelling rules: ko-no-so loses its double s, and te-qa uses q for Thebes' old kʷ sound.

topics.title: Gods on the Tablets
topics.short: po-se-da-o (Poseidon), di-we and di-wo (Zeus), e-ra (Hera), di-wo-nu-so (Dionysus), e-ma-a2 (Hermes) and a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja (Mistress Athena) appear by name.
topics.trouble: Students assume the Olympians were invented later. Several are named on the tablets, though we know little of the myths told about them then.

topics.title: The Palace Economy
topics.short: The tablets track what came in and went out: flocks and wool, oil and perfume, rations for workers, bronze for smiths, chariots and armor.
topics.trouble: Students expect stories or letters. The tablets are accounts, and their value is in the patterns they show across thousands of entries.

topics.title: The Wanax and the Lawagetas
topics.short: The wa-na-ka (wanax) ruled the palace state; the ra-wa-ke-ta (lawagetas) ranked next; a qa-si-re-u (later basileus, king) was a lesser local official.
topics.trouble: Students read qa-si-re-u as "king". In the tablets the basileus was a minor official; the word rose in status only after the palaces fell.

topics.title: Offerings to the Gods
topics.short: Tablets list offerings of oil, honey and gold vessels to gods; Pylos tablet Tn 316 records gold vessels and people brought to Zeus, Hera and others.
topics.trouble: Students take one reading of a hard tablet as fact. Some scholars read Tn 316's people as human offerings; others as servants given to the gods' service. The text does not settle it.

topics.title: What the Tablets Don't Tell
topics.short: No poems, laws, letters or histories survive in Linear B; the tablets record one season's business, so much about these people remains unknown.
topics.trouble: Students expect the tablets to confirm Homer or tell of the Trojan War. They name no war, no Agamemnon and no history at all.

topics.title: Linear A: Where and What
topics.short: The Minoan script, used about 1800 to 1450 BC: about 1,400 short inscriptions, most from Hagia Triada, Zakros, Chania and Phaistos.
topics.trouble: Students think Linear A is a large body of texts. It is small: about 7,400 signs in all, mostly short lists, many damaged.

topics.title: Signs Shared with Linear B
topics.short: Many Linear A signs look like Linear B signs, so scholars read them with the Linear B values by convention; this is a working guess about sounds.
topics.trouble: Students treat Linear A sound values as known. They are borrowed from Linear B on the assumption that the sounds carried over with the shapes, which is likely for many signs but not proved.

topics.title: Linear A Numbers and Fractions
topics.short: Linear A counts with the same decimal marks as Linear B and also has fraction signs; J as one half is widely accepted, while values for the others are proposed.
topics.trouble: Students give every fraction sign a firm value. Only a few are widely agreed; the rest are proposals worked out from how the numbers add up.

topics.title: Ku-ro, the Total
topics.short: The word read ku-ro stands before a number that equals the sum of the list above it, so it is widely accepted to mean "total"; ki-ro also recurs in lists, its meaning uncertain.
topics.trouble: Students think knowing ku-ro means we can read Linear A. We know what the word does from the arithmetic, not what language it belongs to.

topics.title: The Libation Formula
topics.short: Stone offering tables from sanctuaries repeat a set of words, such as a-sa-sa-ra-me (also ja-sa-sa-ra-me), i-pi-na-ma and si-ru-te; their meanings are unknown.
topics.trouble: Students treat a-sa-sa-ra-me as a known goddess's name. Many have guessed; the word is recognized because it recurs, not because it is understood.

topics.title: Why Linear A Can't Be Read Yet
topics.short: The texts are few and short, the Minoan language matches no known language, and there is no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone.
topics.trouble: Students think more cleverness is all it takes. Without more texts, a related known language or a bilingual, there is not enough to test a reading.

topics.title: How to Judge a Decipherment Claim
topics.short: A good decipherment makes testable predictions, reads the whole corpus the same way, fits place names and new finds, and convinces specialists.
topics.trouble: Students are persuaded by a few words that seem to match. Claims to read Linear A appear every few years; none has met these tests or been accepted.

topics.title: Linear A and Linear B Side by Side
topics.short: The same sign shapes, different languages: what we know about each script, what we don't, and why Linear B could be read when Linear A cannot.
topics.trouble: Students think Linear A and Linear B are two languages written the same way, or the same language. They share signs, but Linear B writes Greek and Linear A an unknown language.
